profile.title: Nutrition Assessment and Counseling for Fragile Early Behavior Change in a 26-Year-Old with Prediabetes, Chronic Pain, and Food Insecurity
profile.summary: This case presents Oscar Kihn, a 26-year-old uninsured man with new prediabetes, chronic low back pain, a 2020 brain injury, and mild anemia, who presents warm and chatty but reluctant to disclose medication overuse, prior heavy drinking, or unreported supplement/opioid use. It teaches learners to conduct a nontransactional diet/OTC-medication history that surfaces a patient-vs-chart mismatch (unlabeled iron pills and rationed hydrocodone-acetaminophen not reflected in the record), to formulate a food-insecurity-sensitive nutrition diagnosis, and to use motivational interviewing to support a fragile early behavior change while recognizing when findings exceed dietetics scope and require referral.
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in Somerville, NJ (patient notes it's noisy because he shares the house with six family members)

patient.name: Oscar Kihn
patient.occupation: Part-time stock associate at a hardware store
patient.appearance: Calling from a cramped bedroom with a mattress visible behind him and muffled household noise in the background; leans forward chatty and smiling, occasionally rubbing his lower back or pausing mid-sentence before laughing it off; dressed in a hardware store polo like he's about to head to a shift.

persona.personality: Warm, talkative, eager to be liked, quick with a joke or a compliment; proud of small wins but quietly afraid they won't last.
persona.communicationStyle: Chatty and informal, uses plain everyday language, asks the student personal questions and tries to connect; pivots to sports, church, or jokes whenever money, pain pills, or his drinking history come up; gets a little defensive if he senses judgment about his diet or budget.
persona.emotionalState: Anxious underneath a friendly surface — worried the prediabetes diagnosis means he's 'going downhill,' proud of recent changes but scared one bad week will undo them, and embarrassed about things he hasn't told anyone yet.
persona.background: Oscar is a 26-year-old from Somerville, NJ, who works part-time stocking shelves at a hardware store and lives with six other family members in one house. He left high school with some vocational training but never did a four-year degree, which makes him a little self-conscious around people he sees as more educated. His closest community is his church's young adults group — he calls them 'basically my second family' — they do potlucks, give each other rides, and pray for one another. He likes pickup basketball at the church gym on weekends when his back allows, and he keeps a dog-eared devotional booklet his small-group leader gave him in his truck. He's saving spare cash in a jar toward a used car so he doesn't have to keep borrowing his cousin's.
speechExamples: Yeah I cut way back on the soda these last few weeks — pretty proud of that, honestly.
My back's been bad since '18, hurt it moving stuff at an old job.
Ha, my brain's got a few potholes since 2020, I just laugh it off now.
I eat what we can afford, man, not everybody can buy the fancy stuff.
So wait, what do YOU usually eat on a work night? I'm nosy like that.
concerns: Worried the prediabetes news means he's 'going downhill' like an uncle who lost his foot to diabetes
Afraid of being judged for using the food pantry and buying cheap food
Nervous about mixing OTC pain meds without really knowing the limits
Scared the 'good streak' he started a few weeks ago will fall apart like it has before

scenario.studentBrief: You are a dietetics student conducting a telehealth nutrition visit with Oscar Kihn, a 26-year-old man recently diagnosed with prediabetes. He is calling from home. This is a follow-up nutrition assessment tied to his prediabetes care plan. Review the available health record before the call.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Follow-up nutrition visit for newly diagnosed prediabetes
scenario.openingLine: Hey, thanks for calling — yeah so, I guess I'm here 'cause they told me I'm prediabetic now. I already started cutting back on soda the last few weeks though, pretty proud of that.
tasks: Take a focused diet, meal pattern, and supplement/OTC medication history
Review available vitals, anthropometrics, and lab results relevant to his nutrition status
Identify a nutrition diagnosis related to his prediabetes and current eating pattern
Explore barriers to healthy eating such as budget, food access, pain, and health literacy
Use motivational interviewing to support and reinforce his recent small changes, and note anything that needs follow-up with his primary care provider

objectives.text: Elicit a complete and accurate OTC medication, prescription, and supplement history despite low health literacy and reluctance to disclose, including unlabeled or informally-sourced products.
Interpret vitals, anthropometrics, and relevant labs (HbA1c, fasting glucose, CBC/hemoglobin, BMP) to characterize nutrition status in the context of prediabetes and anemia.
Formulate a nutrition diagnosis addressing excessive carbohydrate/energy intake relative to needs, grounded in a focused diet and meal pattern history.
Identify and discuss practical barriers to healthy eating, including food insecurity, tight household budget, chronic pain, fatigue, and low health literacy.
Apply motivational interviewing techniques to affirm and reinforce a fragile, recently-initiated behavior change (reduced soda, evening walking).

Recognize safety-relevant findings outside dietetics scope (overlapping acetaminophen exposure, unreported dizziness, unlabeled supplement use) and determine when to refer to the primary care provider rather than manage directly.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Nutrition diagnosis: Excessive carbohydrate/energy intake relative to needs (NI-5.8/NI-1.3) in a 26-year-old with prediabetes, in the context of food insecurity, chronic pain, and low health literacy, with a fragile early behavior change (reduced soda, started walking).
differential: Prediabetes nutrition-related: excessive carbohydrate/energy intake relative to estimated needs
Inconsistent carbohydrate/meal timing pattern (breakfast skipping, large single evening meal, grazing) contributing to glycemic risk
Food/nutrition-related knowledge deficit regarding portion size and carbohydrate sources (vs. soda-only framing of 'healthy eating')
Inadequate iron intake/possible multifactorial mild anemia (dietary pattern plus unrecorded supplement use)
Limited access to nutritious food (food insecurity, household of 7, pantry reliance)
keyFindings: HbA1c 5.8% (2026-07-02), fasting glucose 98.5 mg/dL — consistent with prediabetes
BMI 26.5 kg/m2 (height 181.2 cm, weight 87 kg), weight up 1.4 kg over about a year
Hemoglobin 11.3 g/dL (mildly low) with mild conjunctival/nail bed pallor on observation
BP 136/90 mmHg; other labs (sodium, potassium, BUN, WBC, platelets) within normal limits
Dietary pattern: skips breakfast, large shared starchy/processed dinner (spaghetti with jarred sauce, peanut butter sandwiches, fried bologna), vending-machine snacking, soda as primary beverage
Reports taking a dollar-store multivitamin 'most days' and protein powder in milk; chart lists only the multivitamin as his supplement
Patient reveals in conversation that he also takes unlabeled iron pills from a cousin a few times a week when tired, not disclosed to any provider — a mismatch with the chart record of supplement use
Reports ibuprofen 400mg PRN 'a few times a week' and daily/near-daily acetaminophen 325mg; on gentle questioning admits sometimes exceeding the ibuprofen label dose

On further exploration, discloses rationing a few leftover acetaminophen-hydrocodone 300mg/5mg tablets every couple of weeks, creating unrecognized overlapping acetaminophen intake with his daily OTC acetaminophen use
Reports new-onset dizziness he has not mentioned to any provider, plausibly related to anemia and breakfast skipping
Food insecurity indicators: household of 7, uninsured, intermittent food pantry use, budget-driven food choices
Currently in action stage of change: reduced soda intake and started evening walking a few weeks ago, but expresses low confidence this will stick
plan: Complete ADIME nutrition assessment: diet history (24-hr recall/typical day), anthropometrics, review of labs/vitals, OTC medication and supplement history, psychosocial/food access screen

Establish nutrition diagnosis(es) using PES statement format addressing excessive carbohydrate/energy intake relative to needs related to food insecurity and low health literacy, as evidenced by dietary pattern and HbA1c/BMI trend

Nutrition intervention: patient-centered education on balanced plate/portion concepts (not just 'cutting soda'), practical low-cost carbohydrate-aware meal ideas using foods already in his pattern (spaghetti, peanut butter, canned/boxed pantry items), consistent meal timing including a feasible breakfast option

Use motivational interviewing to affirm and reinforce his soda reduction and walking as self-directed, fragile but real progress; collaboratively set one small, concrete next step rather than overhauling his diet
Explore and validate food access barriers; connect him with food pantry days he already uses and any available food assistance resources without judgment

Flag for referral to primary care / pharmacist: overlapping acetaminophen exposure (OTC acetaminophen plus acetaminophen-hydrocodone), ibuprofen use exceeding label directions, unlabeled iron supplement use of unknown dose/source, and new unreported dizziness — dietetics scope is to identify and refer, not adjust these medications
Recommend recheck of hemoglobin/anemia workup and vital signs given reported dizziness, in coordination with his medical provider
Monitoring/follow-up: schedule nutrition follow-up visit to reassess diet pattern, weight, and sustainability of soda/walking changes; coordinate with primary care on labs and medication safety
redFlags: Overlapping acetaminophen intake from near-daily OTC acetaminophen plus intermittent acetaminophen-hydrocodone tablets, raising hepatotoxicity risk if combined without awareness
Ibuprofen use sometimes exceeding labeled dose in an uninsured patient with no routine monitoring (GI/renal risk)
Unlabeled, unsourced iron supplement use of unknown dose that could mask or complicate anemia work-up
New, unreported dizziness that has not been evaluated
Mild anemia (Hgb 11.3) that is undiagnosed in cause and not yet linked to his supplement or dietary pattern
educationPoints: Prediabetes can often be addressed with practical shifts in meal timing and portioning rather than buying special or expensive foods
A consistent breakfast or morning snack may help with energy, afternoon sweet cravings, and glycemic stability
All over-the-counter medications and supplements, including ones from family members, are important to share with a care team because they can add up or interact
Small, self-directed changes (like reducing soda and adding walks) are meaningful progress worth protecting with realistic, low-pressure next steps
Food pantry use and budget-driven food choices are common and nothing to be ashamed of; nutrition guidance can work within that reality

mismatches.patientClaim: Oscar reports taking a dollar-store multivitamin most days and protein powder after work as his only supplements (h25, h27)
mismatches.recordEvidence: Nutrition Intake Questionnaire / supplement inventory lists only the dollar-store multivitamin and protein powder; no mention of iron pills from a cousin
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patients may under-report unlabeled or informally-sourced supplements (e.g., pills from family) because they don't think of them as 'real' medication; a gentle, nonjudgmental supplement inventory can surface sources that complicate anemia work-up.

mismatches.patientClaim: Oscar reports taking ibuprofen 400mg 'as needed, usually a few times a week' and acetaminophen 325mg 'daily or near-daily' (h21, h22)
mismatches.recordEvidence: Pharmacy Fill History Summary shows ibuprofen refill rate above a 'few times a week' pattern and acetaminophen fills consistent with near-daily use, suggesting higher actual intake than initially reported
mismatches.teachingPoint: Self-reported OTC medication frequency often undercounts actual use, especially when patients fear being judged; cross-checking fill history helps identify overlapping acetaminophen exposure that needs referral.
